speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This Bill is also about fortifying Singapore, specifically to protect our critical infrastructures and certain buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today’s terrorists typically target crowded places or iconic buildings, so that they can take out as many lives as possible and make a huge statement with their acts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Their aim is to create fear and upend our way of life in the ideological battle between their and our values.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In August this year, vehicle-ramming attacks in Catalonia, Spain, killed 16 people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The terrorists behind the attacks had also planned to bomb iconic buildings in Barcelona.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2011, a car bomb exploded in front of government buildings in Oslo, which included the Prime Minister’s office.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It killed eight people and significantly damaged several buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2008, the Marriott Hotel in Islamabad was targeted by a massive truck bomb.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It was stopped by the hotel’s vehicle security barrier 40 metres from the front of the hotel, which blunted the attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But it was not enough; the blast left a huge crater outside the hotel and 54 people dead.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These incidents testify to the importance of adequately protecting our infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Despite heightened alert and best efforts by the security agencies, the attacks had still succeeded to varying degrees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been cited as a target in jihadist publications and videos.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Attacks have been plotted against us, such as the one involving Marina Bay Sands last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There has been a significant rise in the number of radicalised individuals detained.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Terrorist attention on this region is also growing, fuelled by conflict in areas like Marawi.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Realistically, we cannot expect to uncover and foil every terrorist plot.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is why our response has to be comprehensive, covering not just pre-emptive action by the security agencies, but infrastructure protection as well, to mitigate the consequences of a successful attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the past two years, the Government has expanded closed-circuit television (CCTV) coverage, enhanced border protection, upgraded the response capabilities of our security forces and mobilised the community, among other measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Public Order Act was amended in April to require organisers of large-scale events to take necessary security measures to protect the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This Bill is a continuation of our counterterrorism efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It has to be seen against the backdrop of the evolving and worsening threat, and the cognisance that no single approach can effectively deal with it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill aims to protect key infrastructure against attacks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Indeed, measures like vehicle barriers and hardening of structures and of glazing, are a key line of defence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can both deter attacks and blunt the force of an attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Building security is the responsibility of building owners, and it will remain so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They know their needs and operations best and are responsible for the safety of their tenants and the public who visit their buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But for certain buildings, the risk and impact of an attack are much more significant, for example, those with high public footfall, or are iconic of our society and way of life.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In these cases, it is in the public interest for the Government to be proactive in ensuring that appropriate security measures are put in place to safeguard lives and property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) already works with owners of critical infrastructure and selected commercial buildings, to take security into account upfront in the development process, by integrating into the building design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Current laws, however, do not provide us with the authority to mandate such infrastructure protection; we have relied on engagement and persuasion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While such an approach has worked reasonably well so far, given the worsening threat environment, the Government has assessed that we should establish a clear regulatory framework to more systematically protect Singapore’s infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will also provide more transparency and clarity about the requirements and processes for building owners and developers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is impractical to turn the whole of Singapore into a fortress.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In deciding which buildings to regulate, we have to consider the risk to the public, the national interest and the cost to businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A successful strike on critical infrastructure will disrupt essential services, such as power, water or transport.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: An attack on large buildings with high public footfall could result in mass casualties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Iconic buildings are also attractive targets for terrorists because of their international reputation or significance to Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While any building could be a target, it is clearly not practical to require every building in Singapore to undergo security-by-design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For buildings that need not undergo security-by-design, the Bill enables MHA to introduce or to issue directives for owners to put in place appropriate security measures against the risk of a terrorist attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If an attack is imminent, emergency orders may also be issued to protect these buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, the Bill will enhance powers to protect sensitive locations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These locations are currently declared under the Protected Areas and Protected Places Act (PAPPA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of them are critical infrastructure or military areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will go through each of these three aspects covered by the Bill in some detail.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Security-by-design is a process to ensure that security is designed into the building design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It attempts to mitigate security risks through good building design and incorporates security measures upfront into the building features.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Examples of such security measures include: (a) hardening of structural elements, such as walls and columns, to resist bomb blast effects; (b) providing for a stand-off distance using security barriers to prevent unauthorised vehicles from coming close to the building; and (c) combining security technology with operational processes, such as monitoring CCTVs, operating access control systems, or implementing security procedures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A key benefit of security-by-design is that security is effectively incorporated into the building without overly compromising other factors, such as the form and function of the building.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is generally more cost-effective because good design can reduce or even eliminate the need for some security measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 5 will empower the Minister for Home Affairs to appoint a Commissioner of Infrastructure Protection.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Commissioner will be responsible for the administration of the Bill, including security-by-design requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part 4 of the Bill, or clauses 32 to 48, details the security-by-design requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In Part 5, clauses 51 to 53 allow the Commissioner to issue directives to address non-compliance with security-by-design requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Minister will designate the buildings that need to undergo security-by-design in the interests of public safety and public security, or national interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clause 34, such new buildings that have not yet been built will be designated as Special Developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will need to undergo security-by-design before construction starts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clause 41, existing buildings will be designated as Special Infrastructures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will need to undergo security-by-design when they undertake major renovations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Owners of such infrastructures would already be familiar with security-by-design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the past decade, MHA has worked closely with Government agencies to identify critical infrastructures and incorporate security into their design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As for the second group of buildings, new developments that have potential of high public footfall will be designated as "Special Developments".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will be identified based on objective criteria, such as gross floor area, whether they are zoned for commercial, community or mixed use, and whether they are in certain planning areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In clause 34, the Bill makes clear that we will publish the criteria which will be used to designate a class of Special Developments under a gazette order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The order will require any new developments that meet the criteria to undergo security-by-design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We may also designate new developments that do not meet the high public footfall criteria but are iconic as Special Developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For existing buildings that meet the high public footfall criteria, they will generally be designated as Special Infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA will engage each owner and assess the need for security measures, taking into consideration the building’s actual land use and profile.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Any further requirements to be imposed will be reasonable and practical, taking into account the fact that these are existing and not new buildings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will be as transparent as possible about the buildings that we will designate as Special Developments or Special Infrastructures and inform the building owners as early as we can.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 32 describes who will be the responsible person of a Special Development or Special Infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After a new development or existing building is designated, clauses 35 and 42 require responsible persons to submit a security plan to the Commissioner for approval, before specified works can be carried out.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The term “specified works” is defined in clause 2.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For Special Developments, specified works refer to key construction works, such as those affecting the foundation, retaining structure, substructure or super structure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For Special Infrastructures, specified works refer to an extension of the premises, or major renovation works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 33 explains what the security plan should cover.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It should include the risk assessment and necessary security measures for the designated premises and must be prepared by a competent person approved by MHA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For Special Infrastructures, a security plan to be approved by the Commissioner is required for major renovation works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The term “major renovation” is defined in clause 2 and broadly refers to works that may introduce new security risks, for example, works at publicly accessible areas, the perimeter, or involving critical assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A security plan to assess the risks, adjust existing security measures or add new measures will be required.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The security plan may be required to cover areas outside of the specified works, so that security risks to the designated premises may be addressed adequately.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The scope of such security measures will be reasonable, for example, to install or upgrade access control or video surveillance systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will be an offence to commence specified works without an approved security plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clause 51, the Commissioner may direct the responsible person to stop any specified works and take actions to comply with the requirement to submit a security plan for approval.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This requirement will also be incorporated in the Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA’s) conditions when granting provisional permission to developers to carry out works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After the Commissioner approves the security plan, works can commence and the security measures in the approved security plan must be implemented.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 39 and 46 require the responsible person to submit a Certificate of Works Completion (CWC) and obtain the Commissioner’s approval.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The CWC certifies that required security measures have been implemented by the time specified works are completed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The CWC must be prepared by an approved competent person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 40 explains that Special Developments become Special Infrastructures once the CWC is approved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If the specified works require a Temporary Occupation Permit or Certificate of Statutory Completion from the Building and Construction Authority (BCA), these cannot be obtained without an approved CWC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After the CWC is approved, clauses 40 and 47 require the responsible person to implement the rest of the security measures and maintain every security measure in accordance with the approved security plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Failure to do so will be an offence punishable with a fine of up to $20,000 or two years’ jail or both.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 38 and 45 allow flexibility through regulations for security measures in the security plan to be modified after the CWC is approved, for example, due to changes in the owner’s operational needs, or if existing measures need to be adjusted because of new specified works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clauses 52 and 53, the Commissioner may direct the responsible person to take actions to rectify non-compliance with the approved security plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second key aspect of the Bill is the introduction of directives and orders to protect buildings against terrorist attacks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Commissioner may issue security directives to Special Developments and Special Infrastructures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clause 54, the Commissioner may direct the responsible person of a Special Infrastructure to implement and maintain specific security measures, if it is necessary to address any security risk.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This could be because the Special Infrastructure does not have any approved security plan, meaning that it did not previously undergo security-by-design, or because the approved security plan does not address emerging or new security risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clause 55, the Commissioner may issue security directives to publicly accessible premises which have not been designated as Special Infrastructures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The purpose is to be able to direct persons to implement specific security measures to address the risk of a terrorist attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such measures could include installing vehicle security barriers, or improving CCTV coverage and allowing the Police to view the feeds in order to protect the building against a terrorist attack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These measures will also not include the strengthening of structural elements against blast effects, which typically involve major structural modifications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 56 makes non-compliance with security directives an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also an offence if the person continues not to comply with the security directive even after he is convicted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Security directives are intended as a last resort.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where a building is assessed to be at risk, MHA and the Police will first engage building owners to develop practical security measures and encourage them to undertake those measures voluntarily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But if the building owner is resistant and there is a potential risk to public safety and security, directives will be used.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The order can require security measures, such as preparing and implementing contingency plans, installing temporary security measures, and deploying security guards to restrict access of people and vehicles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The order can also require the temporary closure of a part or the whole of the premises, allowing state forces to access the premises, or for the owner to provide any information relevant to protecting the premises, for example, their building plans, visitor and car park records, or CCTV feeds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under clause 65, if the Minister’s order is not complied with, the Commissioner may enter the premises to carry out the directions in the order and recover the costs from the owners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part 7 provides for appeals to the Minister against certain decisions of the Commissioner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During security-by-design, if the Commissioner rejects the security plan of a Special Development or Special Infrastructure, the responsible person may appeal to the Minister.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Persons issued with security directives under Part 5 may also appeal to the Minister.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In cases where independent technical advice is needed, the Minister may refer the appeal to an Appeal Advisory Board, comprising relevant experts, and appointed under clause 63.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third and final key aspect of the Bill is to enhance powers to protect sensitive locations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most Singaporeans would be familiar with the red warning signs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are sensitive facilities where the movement and conduct of persons need to be controlled for security reasons, for example, border checkpoints, military training camps, and critical infrastructure delivering essential services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The difference between a Protected Area and a Protected Place is that a Protected Place is not accessible to the public without approval from the owner of the place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, only persons with a valid boarding pass or other authorisation may enter those places.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the other hand, the departure halls are Protected Areas and are accessible to the general public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But in both locations, the movement and conduct of people are controlled for security reasons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The purpose of PAPPA is to provide powers to authorities in charge of sensitive locations and their guards to protect their premises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The key provisions of PAPPA remain relevant today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill will repeal PAPPA, enhance the provisions, and port them over to Part 3, or clauses 8 to 31 of this Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Protected Areas and Protected Places declared under the current PAPPA will remain under the new Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So will existing powers for guards to control movement in the Protected Area or Place, conduct searches of persons and property, remove persons and property, and arrest persons by force, if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clauses 12 and 18 make explicit the responsibilities for authorities in charge of Protected Areas and Places.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where guards are deployed, they must be authorised officers to ensure that they have the proper training and authorisation to exercise the powers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The boundaries of Protected Areas and Places must be clearly marked.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For Protected Places, measures must be put in place to prevent unauthorised access.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To address today’s threat environment, the Bill will make two enhancements to the powers for Protected Areas and Protected Places.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first enhancement is to prevent terrorists from carrying out pre-attack surveillance of their targets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Images of Protected Areas and Places can threaten public safety, if used for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can reveal details of security measures, the flow of people and the movement of the guards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means that photos can only be taken if the authority in charge of the Protected Area or Protected Place gives its permission.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will apply to land-based, as well as to aerial photography.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 29 also empowers authorised officers to direct persons to stop taking photos and delete any photos taken.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Signs will be displayed at the perimeter of the Protected Area or Place to indicate that unauthorised photography is prohibited.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similar provisions exist in the Air Navigation Act and the Public Order Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unauthorised photography of Protected Areas and Places by unmanned aerial vehicles is an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Authorised officers designated by the Police under clause 30 will have powers to address such instances of unauthorised photography, such as assuming control of the unmanned aerial vehicle to land it safely and quickly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second enhancement is to deter and detect persons in the surrounding area who pose a security threat to the Protected Area or Protected Place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This could be a person who carries a suspicious bag or parks a truck near the perimeter or loiters near the Protected Area or Place without good reason.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They could also distract the attention of authorised officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Potential attacks overseas have been stopped by vigilant guards in the surrounding area of a sensitive facility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In April this year, police in the United Kingdom (UK) arrested a man near the Prime Minister’s Office on suspicion of preparing to commit an act of terrorism.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It turned out that he was carrying three knives in a rucksack.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When engaging a person in the surrounding area, authorised officers may request for his personal identification and reason for being there.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If the person fails to comply, or does not give a good and lawful reason to be there, the authorised officer may direct him to move on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The authorised officer may also inspect belongings and vehicles, if he reasonably suspects that the person is carrying dangerous items.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 26 makes clear that the powers in clauses 27 and 28 apply only if the surrounding area is specified in the order of the Protected Area or Place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Signs will be displayed at the perimeter of the Protected Area or Place to indicate that the powers apply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA has consulted stakeholders in developing the Bill, including from the built environment sector, such as real estate developers, architects and engineers, as well as owners and operators of critical infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We recognise that the new infrastructure protection framework would require more expertise and resources in the area of building security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the longer term, we will consider making the involvement of PE (PS) in the security-by-design process as a legal requirement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MHA will also publish updated Guidelines for Enhancing Building Security in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will guide building owners on conducting security risk assessments, designing secure buildings and selecting appropriate security measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Centre for Protective Security Studies will conduct training and outreach on the guidelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today, MHA works with selected buildings to integrate security into their design.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other buildings which we deem to be at some risk of terrorist attacks, but which we have not designated as Special Infrastructures, may also be required to put in place security measures, if directed to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But while infrastructure protection measures can mitigate the terrorist threat, they cannot eliminate it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need to step up efforts on all fronts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill must thus be seen as part of a comprehensive national counterterrorism framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes CCTV coverage, border protection, response capabilities of the security forces, as well as the role of the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Indeed, no single initiative or legislation alone can tackle the multifaceted threat of terrorism.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Every Singaporean must stand up to be counted and play our part to safeguard Singapore’s safety and security.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Naturally, owners and occupiers designated as the responsible authorities of protected places are concerned with higher costs associated with such designs, installations and measures.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These may include special materials for protection against blast effects, vehicle barriers, CCTV and security guards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The owners and occupiers of protected places will want more clarity about the burden and apportionment of costs for enhanced security.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, another equally important component for infrastructure protection is the personnel involved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides the security staff, non-security personnel at these facilities should also be trained in how to act to reduce risks and respond in the event of emergencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All staff should be trained with regular drills, and processes must be in place to ensure that the necessary steps and compliance measures are adhered to.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hospitals are a very important part of our infrastructure, along with other more obvious facilities, such as our airports, ports, checkpoints and military installations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They provide an essential service and experience high human traffic daily, which make them potential targets for terrorists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the event of a terror attack, the provision of medical care could be severely disrupted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, medical personnel and equipment are very difficult to replace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I hope that our hospitals will be accorded greater protection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These threats are not merely terrorism-related but include threats from crime and accidents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It goes without saying that appropriate security measures can safeguard lives and property and minimise disruptions to essential services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Having said that, it should also be borne in mind that we should also not go overboard and have the country in perpetual lock-down mode.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We must be able to go about our daily activities efficiently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we cannot live normal lives, the terrorists have already won.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I am in general support of the Bill, I have some queries and concerns to raise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, on Part 3: protected areas and protected places.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill repeals the current Protected Areas and Protected Places Act and re-enacts the same provisions but includes some new provisions as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I assume that this is due to the heightened security environment and inflation over the years, but I appreciate the Minister's clarification on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it is perfectly reasonable to prohibit such actions inside or above the protected area or protected place, the section makes it an offence to take a photograph or make a recording from outside the protected area and protected place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Maps available on the Internet, such as Google Earth, already show such information publicly anyway.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to Part 4: special developments and special infrastructures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill introduces new provisions that certain developments and buildings will be required to have security plans approved by the new Commissioner for Infrastructure Protection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What constitutes a "special development" or "special infrastructure"?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Ministry's press release on 11 September and also the Minister’s Second Reading speech, these buildings would be those which "house essential services, are iconic, or with high human traffic".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 34 states that the Minister will be the one designating "special developments" and "special infrastructures" that need to comply with the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could there be further elaboration on the types and extent of buildings that would need to be designated?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, will all shopping malls be designated?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates, clause 2 of the Bill states that Town Councils would be considered owners of common property for the purpose of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Which part of HDB estates would be deemed "special infrastructures"?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, as far as developments are concerned, the intention is to have security embedded into the facility at the design stage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 35 makes it clear that key structural works cannot commence until the security plan is approved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From a security management perspective, such early emplacement of security concerns is recommended and likely to achieve better outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the design stage, security professionals can work with architects, engineers and facility owners to ensure that security features do not disrupt the overall building aesthetics or the facility's operational needs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clauses 33 provides that the security plans must be prepared by a person approved by the Commissioner for Infrastructure Protection in connection with those works.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the Commissioner accept a security professional who is an employee of the owner or occupier?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Sir, clauses 37 and 44 talk about amendments to approved security plans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The amendments can be initiated by either the building owner or the Commissioner for Infrastructure Protection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, after the Commissioner has approved the security plan, he can change his mind sometime later and require additional measures to be included.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Whether clause 80 is fair will depend on why the amendment to the plan at a later stage was needed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the amendment was due to the negligence of the authorities in the first approval, should the owner be forced to bear the additional cost?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the launch of SGSecure to sensitise, train and mobilise the community in the event of an attack, it is highly relevant that we now take a hard review at the adequacy of our safety protocols and put in place networks, structures, systems and processes to support our nation's effort in the constant battle against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I am most supportive of this Bill, I would like to raise some points for the Minister's consideration.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, some of these points have already been covered to some extent by the Second Minister in her very thorough opening speech, but I hope that she will be open also to considering the points raised over the next few minutes or so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This reinforces the importance given to securing our key installations and properties against possible incursions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the appointment of a coordinating Commissioner and his/her team is a step in the right direction, the question of how coordination can be done across multiple agencies needs to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, what are the criteria for the Commissioner's appointment and what will be the extent of his/her power?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would he or she be vested with authority to coordinate the activities of different agencies that are now responsible for infrastructure protection?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And is the Ministry considering setting up a dedicated Agency for Infrastructure Protection to execute the duties of the role?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would like now to move on to clause 8 which states that the Minister will be vested with wide-ranging power to declare any premises in Singapore as a protected area if it is deemed necessary to control the movement and conduct of persons on the premises.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I appreciate that exigencies might require swift responses from the Government, would the Government consider building in safeguards to protect against potential compromise of stakeholders' interests?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In its current form, the Bill clarifies only the purpose and intent of the protected area but does not specify the criteria that would be used to determine if a premises should come under protection.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As opposed to the current broad interpretation that an area can come under protection upon application of its owner and by volition of the Minister, would the Ministry consider publishing guidelines that lay out the framework to determine whether an area will be put under protection, and also, how would the scope of protection relate to the strategic importance of the asset and level of threat?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a related note, if a designated protected area incorporates a mix of residential and commercial interests, such as, say, the Marina Bay Financial Centre, how would the designation of the protected area impact the interest of residents and businesses in that area?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clause 18 of the Bill highlights that only "authorised officers" are to be deployed to guard protected places.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A closer reading of the Bill reveals that "authorised officers" are interpreted broadly to encompass personnel from various divisions of the Home Team and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), as well as Auxiliary Police Officers and security guards.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe, Mr Speaker, that we need to ensure that "authorised officers" who are protecting the installations are adequately and adeptly trained to spot, manage and neutralise potential terrorists.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and SAF have specialised personnel who are trained to protect key installations, it would be hard to reconcile that an Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) officer, though with due respect, or security guard deployed by a commercial security firm would possess that same level of training to be a deterrent for would-be terrorists.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider implementing a training curriculum and a certification process to ensure that all personnel deployed to guard key installations have the right level of competence and skill to discharge their duties?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would differentiate a casual security guard from a specialised officer that has been trained and prepared for guarding protected places.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of these devices, as mentioned by the Second Minister herself earlier, would include video or surveillance devices in the vicinity of the building, barriers to prevent vehicular threats to crowds or building structures, specially-reinforced concrete walls that do not collapse easily, and fireproof claddings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry intend to conduct a safety audit, as it were, on existing buildings to ensure that building owners are compelled to rectify security shortcomings to mitigate collateral damage from terrorist attacks?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, would there be guidelines for public agencies, such as Town Councils and HDB, on enhancing public safety in HDB estates, as well as guidelines for owners of commercial properties on what they could and, perhaps, should do to deter would-be attacks?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was wondering if this concept could be expanded to include perhaps the notion of "security-by-redesign" for existing buildings and properties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we have avoided terrorist attacks on Singapore soil thus far, we must not stop enhancing our defence against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Terrorists evolve their tactics quickly to stay one step ahead of security and law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Cars and lorries are now used just as effectively as explosives to cause carnage, fear and deadly divisions in many countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We saw these in Finland, the UK and Spain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These will involve additional costs and resources for businesses and may result in some inconvenience as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, a successful attack involves a far graver cost, and not just for businesses, but for everyone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill is not alone in its bid to strengthen Singapore’s line against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Counter-Terrorism Committee under the United Nations has similarly called for greater partnership between the public and private sectors to secure critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can understand the concerns on costs because there can be a long tail of them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The costs involved will include consultancy, implementation and long-term maintenance and replacement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the Ministry better help our businesses to manage these costs effectively so that it will not be passed down to tenants and customers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, the Ministry’s regulatory costs could also increase to ensure that the security measures are in working condition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry itself better manage such longer-term costs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because the measures that might be needed can be extensive, there is value for a prescribed code, much like a building code.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This allows companies to know what is expected of them as part of forward business planning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, this might then become an ironically useful guide for terrorists.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, there must be sufficient consultants and capacity in the Ministry to ensure that building owners are not unduly delayed in seeking approvals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to ensure that security officers are kept updated on these new measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would new forms of training be required and refresher training be introduced to help existing security officers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is also a consequential need for a pool of capable and well-trained staff in facilities management who can ensure that the new security measures implemented are in good working order.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will also need the security agencies to have sufficient resources to audit the buildings, the list of which perhaps will only grow with time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The powers to stop unauthorised photography are needed to stem terrorist surveillance and reconnaissance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Do the powers also extend to publishing of such photos?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What measures or education efforts will be taken to increase awareness?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, laws alone will not solve all our security issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There will still be many buildings holding thousands of people and of iconic and important value but not included within the guidelines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we know it is unwise to barricade every building and line every street with bollards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must secure whatever we can, prudently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is another ring of defence to complement our SGSecure work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The best defence is still an engaged and resilient citizenry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Enhancement of security measures to buildings and provision of powers to security personnel to better protect Singapore’s infrastructure against security risks is timely, in light of the prevalence of indiscriminate terror attacks carried out globally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, I applaud the initiative to rope in the business community as part of the shared effort to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These circumstances include a catch-all provision prescribing if that person, in the opinion of the authorised officer, does not have a good and lawful reason to enter or to be in that protected area or place, or is acting in a suspicious manner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe there are less concerns when these powers are given to Police Officers, but there is concern that this Bill indicates that such powers can be given to security officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The training a Police Officer receives is very different from the training a security officer receives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, there is now a stronger focus on the role of security officers in our fight against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This duty ought to be shared by all, including businesses, premises owners and developers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as shared by Members who have spoken before me, there have been concerns by building owners on rising operational costs when additional security measures have to be put in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is less concern for new buildings or those undergoing major renovations since they can factor in such costs during the initial stages, but more so when we issue directives or orders for existing buildings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also applaud their focus on the “Security-by-Design” process, and I understand we are one of the first few countries in the world to legislate the need for such a process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe it is important and necessary to include the entire community in efforts to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By working together, we can keep Singapore secure.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, to ensure that the desired outcomes of the Bill be achieved, it is important that other aspects related to the implementation of the Bill be looked into as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The effectiveness of the Bill will depend on the capabilities and competency of the security officers which, currently, vary widely.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our ICA and SPF officers are well-trained and equipped with relevant training, such as the Threat-Oriented Person Screening Integrated System (TOPSIS) profiling and Red-Team simulations, to ensure that they always maintain their edge in executing their duties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The 42,000 officers diverge on demographics, education and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the risk of over generalising things, may I propose that we categorise them into three separate groups?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the one hand, we have officers who are fit and highly competent.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Bouncers, event security officers fit into this category, which is not unlike the APO (E) scheme currently available for APOs who do not need to carry a weapon.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For this group, we should treat them as APOs and they should command a premium salary.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They would have to undergo annual refresher courses and physical fitness tests.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For these officers, taking every extra module subjects them to undue stress because of language difficulties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These officers should be allowed to serve as security officers at sites deemed low risk, and we thank MHA and the Police Licensing and Regulatory Department (PLRD) for taking the first step towards this consideration, as reflected in the proposed Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important to note that my recommendation does not discriminate this group of workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should any of these officers like to upgrade themselves, by all means they can do so.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the middle, we have a group of officers who, though not as fit, may be able to take on other duties, like first aid, lift rescue and firefighting.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Buyers today already expect them to do so, without properly prescribing them in the contracts, nor paying for it.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This should sit on top of their basic pay.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I firmly believe that if we variegate the jobs in the security industry in this manner, we will create a proper career path for our security officers with meaningful pay.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After all, none of us would like to work in an industry where everyone has the same job scope.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Related to this is the need to have better working conditions and employment terms and benefits for our private security officers which can lead to better work performance.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unless a decisive effort is made to improve the working conditions and mandating better employment benefits, it will be difficult to attract younger workers into the industry.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I would like to ask MHA what are the plans to improve working conditions of the security officers and to consider my proposals above to attract younger people to be security officers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, I would like MHA to consider having basic security requirements in residential areas, such as condominiums, that will require the use of technology to improve security with less reliance on headcount.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though a set of guidelines on enhancing building security by MHA and BCA is available, the take-up rate can be further improved if some of these requirements are made mandatory in these residential developments.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of these mandated security requirements should involve the use of technology, such as next-generation visitor management systems, using more smart cameras with surveillance software and smart analytics, perimeter detection that would reduce the need for patrolling, cloud-based reporting for incident reports to be sent to key decision-makers at short notice and having a remote command centre that could optimise manpower deployment on the ground.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a start, by properly assessing the security needs of a site, suitably hardening first before prescribing security manpower will definitely go a long way in enhancing security outcomes for any site and also increase productivity almost instantly.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In short, I would like to propose MHA mandating some of these security risk assessments for residential areas as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Alternatively, MHA could also allow building owners not under the select building scheme to opt-in to meet the requirement or standard of the security measures under the category of Selected Buildings.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would MHA be able to provide the support they require to conform to the prescribed security standards?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have made some suggestions that would complement the efforts undertaken by the Infrastructure Protection Bill as these areas would have a direct impact in achieving the desired outcome under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is timely that we are stepping up security for key buildings and places with high human traffic to counter threats and keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If so, how is the Ministry planning to address the supply shortage whilst ensuring the quality of new APOs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like my fellow Labour Member of Parliament (MP), Mr Zainal Sapari, I am concerned with the manpower shortage, which does have a negative impact on our security officers, including fatigue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask how the Ministry plans to attract more Singaporeans into the sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The manpower crunch, coupled with the projected increase in demand for security officers, makes it clear that we must turn to technology to fill the gap.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, the use of smart video technology and motion sensors can help reduce labour-intensive patrol work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Smart video technology and motion sensors can pick up movements at the perimeter and analyse if they present a threat to the building.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my constituency, the Orchard Road Business Association has been encouraging hotels, retail buildings and offices to harness technology, such as AI-enabled facial recognition, when upgrading their security systems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the cost of implementing such advanced security technologies may be prohibitive for some building owners.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While new developments can incorporate the new security requirements into their design, older buildings may face a far heftier price tag if retrofitting works are extensive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure that Members of this House have all taken part in a fire drill before and, indeed, it is essential for all buildings to have their own evacuation plans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, such evacuations are often planned in insolation by the building’s management.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I was a Police commander and asked to see the fire evacuation plans of buildings in the city centre, I was surprised to find that every building had designated the same small grass patch in the vicinity as its assembly area.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Surely, the space would not be enough if everyone from every building gathers there at the same time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is why coordination, sharing of information and joint exercises are important.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, I am strongly in favour of the Bill’s intent to safeguard our nation’s key areas and buildings from terrorist threats.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we cannot think of infrastructure protection in isolation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must consider the cost of complying to the new laws and whether our security officers are well-equipped to protect our infrastructures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Infrastructure Protection Bill is, indeed, all about pre-emptive measures to protect critical infrastructural facilities against the increasing threats of terrorism.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I am concerned about how we are going to achieve the balance between our security needs and public convenience.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we overdo it, we may end up with protected areas which are operated like a prison.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, if our protection measures are insufficient, such lapses could invite exploitations by terrorists.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This could be a better solution than relying heavily on hardware, such as physical protective installations, which are also necessary.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The use of big data analytical digital techniques, for example, would be useful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have been fortunate in that our neighbouring countries have been working closely with us to cripple such attempts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such cases, the scope for infrastructure defence will be limited due to the destructive powers of such weapons.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   It is said that “As virtue rises one foot, vice rises 10”.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The enemies are in the dark but we are in the open.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, we must take pre-emptive measures to protect our infrastructural facilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Only by doing this can we effectively prevent and fight against terror.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Hence, early detection of self-radicalised individuals, their education and rehabilitation are important countermeasures as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must stay united and harmonious as a community in order to deter extremism, intolerance and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All races must keep constantly reminding one another that our religions and ideologies promote peace and love for our fellow men.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our fight is against terrorism, not against any religion nor any race.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should leverage upon our well-trained, multiracial, multi-religious National Service (NS)men, active and reservists, and update them regularly with counterterrorism skills to expand on security measures on the ground.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They raised many useful points which I shall address.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think Members agree that all of us bear a share of that burden.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Much of the cost of strengthening protection and enhancing security response is borne directly by the Government.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members will agree that safety and security are not only in our collective interest, they also impact the bottom line interests of businesses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this high threat environment, building owners and developers recognise that ensuring the security of their buildings is part and parcel of carrying out business.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A recent survey by the World Economic Forum found that business leaders in Singapore see terrorist attacks as their top global risk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They know that if the security of the building is breached, the damage to property could be much more costly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why even without the Bill, many buildings today already put in place security measures, like CCTVs and vehicle barriers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of these security measures do not involve complex systems and are maintained as part of the buildings’ other facilities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, security-by-design can offer cost savings to businesses in the longer term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When security measures are properly planned and seamlessly integrated into the design of the building, the use of technology, such as CCTV and access control systems, coupled with the appropriate processes, can help save on manpower cost.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The flow of vehicles can be designed to reduce the risk of an attack to crowded areas and minimise or even eliminate the need for bollards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The security requirements under the Bill also apply only to designated buildings, and not all buildings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Based on the proposed criteria, we expect a handful of new developments each year to be affected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I should add that not all of this cost is attributable to the design process per se, since all buildings have to be fitted with some security measures in any case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Also, given that MHA will try to make known as early as possible which buildings need to undergo security-by-design, developers will likely factor in the cost of security measures in their bid price for the land.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Darryl David is right to point out the need to ensure that buildings which are not designated as Special Developments and Special Infrastructures are also protected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Directives and orders offer a calibrated way to safeguard these buildings when a specific security risk has been identified, without having to impose security-by-design on all buildings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can be used to require security measures, such as those mentioned by Mr Darryl David, including security checks and bollards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To help manage the costs, MHA will engage building owners on what security measures would be effective and practical.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Directives will be issued only as a last resort where owners refuse to take action and there is a risk to the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Desmond Choo asked about the kinds of buildings that would be designated Special Developments and Special Infrastructures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is fair that building owners and developers know, as early as possible, whether security-by-design requirements will apply in their own cases.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why we intend to publish the criteria in the Gazette on the types of new developments that will be designated as Special Developments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Essentially, we look at indicators that signal the high likelihood of public footfall being very large.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that will naturally include the size, location and the type of the developments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it will be quite clear through the Gazette which buildings are going to be designated Special Developments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By publishing the criteria in the Gazette, developers and building owners will, therefore, have a good sense if they are affected and those who are unsure can approach MHA for clarification.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As for the timeline, we will inform the building owners as early as we can.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Along with the high public footfall criteria, the details of the security-by-design review process will also be provided to the industry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also be reasonable in the amount of time given to developers and consultants to comply with the requirements under directives and orders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Darryl David asked about the Commissioner of Infrastructure Protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This person would be a senior public servant in the Ministry of Home Affairs who has the necessary professional expertise to make assessments and to coordinate with relevant Home Team agencies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA has been working with selected building owners over the past decade on security-by-design.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there is already a team in place and we will make sure the team is adequately resourced to implement the new requirements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But no new agency needs to be set up for now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about competent persons who need to be approved by the Commissioner to prepare security plans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is no pre-approved list, and we will provide broad guidelines on the requirements that competent persons should meet.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But all will need to be approved for each project because some projects may require special expertise or may be of a sensitive nature.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Developing industry capabilities in security consulting and infrastructure protection is also one of our key priorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are security and blast consultants, as well as other built environment professionals like architects, who are well-versed with security-by-design.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, it is not an idea that is completely new in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over the last decade, a number of projects have already gone through this process.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the Bill extends security-by-design to more new developments, we will build up the pool of competent persons with the new scheme for PE (PS).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also work with the security industry to develop security consulting capabilities as part of the Security Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked about the Commissioner requiring amendments to the security plan after it has been approved and complied with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will only be done if warranted by a security risk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the evolving nature of security threats, the Commissioner must be in a position to order a review of the security plan so that new risks assessed to warrant attention can be mitigated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think Mr Darryl David referred to this as security-by-redesign.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Will there be abortive costs as a result?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will try to avoid this as much as possible, but it may not always be possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have to weigh it against the value of the enhanced security protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is important for us to talk about Developing Industry Capabilities and, in this section, I shall do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked whether the demand for security manpower will increase as a result of the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I mentioned earlier, the key benefit of security-by-design is that it can mitigate security risks upfront in the design of the building and offer cost savings in the longer term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A building that is well-designed for security, with the use of technology, such as CCTV and video analytics integrated upfront, will actually require less manpower to guard.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Not only do we get to save on manpower, this is an opportunity to create new, higher skilled jobs and thereby attract new entrants to the sector.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, guards with an integrated command centre can focus on analysing and responding to incidents over a much larger area, as compared to if they just patrolled on foot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zainal Sapari, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Melvin Yong spoke about the need to train security officers and uplift the industry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, the security industry is a key partner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA is working closely with industry stakeholders and tripartite partners to develop an Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This process has been ongoing for some time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Among other initiatives, the Industry Transformation Map will identify ways to enhance the skills of security officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Currently, security officers guarding Protected Areas and Protected Places must go through a counterterrorism course.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The course was updated earlier this year to be more relevant.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Melvin Yong also pointed out rightly that technology is a key enabler to improve productivity and alleviate manpower challenges in the security industry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member spoke passionately and also suggested enhancing training and job roles and recognising security officers with additional skills.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The ITM will look into this, together with other important related issues they raised, such as attracting more Singaporeans into the industry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nonetheless, the residential building owners can take reference from the criteria used to designate special developments or infrastructures and implement the appropriate security measures themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can also refer to MHA’s Guidelines on Enhancing Building Security in Singapore (GEBSS).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, if they join the Safety and Security Watch Group, a Police Liaison Officer can help their premises undergo a security assessment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Let us now turn to safeguards for the enhanced powers at Protected Areas and Places.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Darryl David asked about the criteria used to declare Protected Areas and Places.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The PAPPA has been in place since 1948.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Typically, the declaration is made at the application of the owner in charge of the sensitive location.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Examples of such locations are military areas and critical infrastructures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They would generally not involve residential or commercial areas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether powers given to the authorised officers are subject to guidelines, and the need to provide security officers with such powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Darryl David also mentioned the need to ensure authorised officers are properly trained.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The private security industry supports the Home Team in ensuring the safety and security of Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the current PAPPA, security officers and APOs can already be deployed to guard Protected Areas and Places and exercise appropriate powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They must, however, first undergo compulsory training, which is mandated by the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This already includes the counterterrorism course which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the Bill, security officers and APOs will have to undergo additional training on how to exercise their proposed new powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will also develop rules of engagement on how these new powers are to be exercised so that the security officers and the APOs know the boundaries within which they operate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, authorised officers will have to carry a map showing the specified surrounding area where they can exercise the proposed powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And because they carry a map, there can be no dispute.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another safeguard: clause 26 provides that if the specified surrounding areas include private property, powers may only be exercised with the consent of the owner or occupier of that private property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clause 31 further provides that when exercising such powers, authorised officers must identify themselves and state their authority to do so, if asked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh supported making unauthorised photography of Protected Areas and Places an offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether such a prohibition was reasonable.
